latin.166: GAR. Observo deinde, nulla necessitate, vel magna utilitate, compulsum Virum Doctum, ut ita anxie et scrupulose subjectum in quatuor significata distingueret; cum quicunque hactenus de primi peccati imputatione locuti sunt, nihil aliud eo nomine intellexerint, ut ex ipsorum scriptis satis patere potest, quam ipsius primi hominis actualem illam transgressionem, qua Dei mandatum de non gustando fructu arboris interdictae violavit. Ut quid igitur opus erat per operosas ambages lectoris animum circumducere, et de peccato in nobis inhaerente, sive corruptione nostra originali, deque imputatione ac poena reatum ipsam consequente verba facere, de quibus in hac disputatione nequaquam agi satis notum est? Non enim quaeritur, utrum nobis omnibus insita sit corruptio, propter quam Deus poenas a nobis exigere merito possit, aut eam nobis imputare, quod nemo Evangelicorum unquam revocavit in dubium: Illud unum in Quaestionem hodie vocari quibusdam volupe est, utrum ex primo illo actuali Adae peccato aliquis reatus, et aliqua poenae dignitas posteris incumbat.
latin.167: PLAC. Primum esto; nulla necessitate, vel magna utilitate compulsus peccatum Adae sic distinxerim, modo distinctio non sit falsa, nec noxia, nec prorsus inutilis, mihi satis est. Utinam in eius libro nihil minus verum, minus utile occurreret! Deinde verum non est, quod ait, quicunque de peccati Adae imputatione locuti sunt, eos nihil aliud eo nomine intellexisse, quam ipsius actualem transgressionem: cujus rei eum admonere debuerunt verba illa mea, ac ut verbis utar Calvini, quia intra nos est, quae, quia causae suae oberant, consulto omisit. Habentur autem illa Calvini verba Comm. in Rom. 5. vs. 17. integrum locum habes supra p. 92. Perit enim differentia quam illic observat inter Christum et Adamum, nisi peccatum Adae, quod nobis imputatur, intra nos sit, seque habeat ut qualitas nobis inhaerens. Tertio, Quod addit de peccato inhaerente ejusque imputatione in hac disputatione non agi, id ipsum dico hoc loco, ac ut dicerem distinctionem illam adhibui. Separandum enim fuit id quod non est inter nos controversum ab eo quod controversum est, removendaque ab hac quaestione omnis ambiguitas et confusio. Quo neglecto qui mihi in hac causa adversantur non me oppugnant, sed umbram suam. Denique quod dicit in quaestionem vocari, utrum ex primo illo actuali Adae peccato aliquis reatus et aliqua poenae dignitas posteris incumbat, vel falsum est, vel ad me non spectat: Doceo enim constanter ex illo peccato aliquem reatum et aliquam poenae dignitatem, si tamen dignitas appellanda est, posteris incumbere: tantum volo non immediate sed mediante corruptione quam peperit, incumbere.
latin.168: GAR. Dicant vero, qui eam prae se ferunt in explicanda Quaestione diligentiam, annon ludificationi deputaturi sint, et praestigiarum loco habituri, si quis ex Novis illis Pontificiorum Doctoribus, qui pacificationis studio provincias et urbes obire credi volunt, blandulus accedat, et in causa momentosa, justificationis puta negocio, consensum cum Evangelicis profiteatur: se nimirum haud invito animo doctrinam amplecti de justificatione per imputatam Christi Domini nostri justitiam, dummodo distinctione adhibita rem explicare liceat; Quia scilicet justitia Christi variis modis accipi potest. 1. Pro actionibus illis ad legis divinae regulam exactissimis, quibus Christus et vivens et moriens plenissimum Patris sui mandatis obsequium praestitit. 2. Pro habituali illa et inhaerente justitia, qua Christi anima splendidissime enituit. 3. Pro justitia interna et habituali, qua unicuique fidelium subjective inest, sed quae justitia Christi merito dici possit, quoniam a Christo, Christique Spiritu, tanquam autore, in nos defluit. Hoc ergo ultimo sensu, agnoscere se, in controversia justificationis, imputationem justitiae Christi: at vero si prima et secunda significatione Christi justitiam accipiamus, se justitiae Christi imputationem nullam agnoscere, sed tanquam absurdam rejicere. Consensum certe in hoc negocio ita explicatum, nemo est, qui non conqueratur Ludibrium esse, potius quam consensum. &c.
latin.169: PLAC. Hoc simile non est appositum, sed oppositum. Huic enim blandulo praestigiatori tam sum dissimilis quam album nigro. Primo ille se enumerasse prae se ferret omnes acceptiones justitiae Christi, cum tamen unam omitteret in justificationis negotio maxime momentosam, qua justitia Christi accipitur pro singulari illa obedientia quam praestitit patiendo mortem, mortem, inquam, crucis; quae vulgo justitia passiva appellatur, et imputari fidelibus ab omnibus Protestantibus sine dubitatione creditur, cum de imputatione justitiae activae, quam solam D. Gar. commemoravit, sit aliqua sententiarum discrepantia, quae pacem Ecclesiae non turbat. Ego vero primi Adae peccati acceptiones omnes recensui, nullam praetermisi. Secundo ille Christi justitiam eo sensu acceptam imputari diceret, quo sensu accepta imputari negatur constanter ab omnibus Protestantibus. Ego vero peccatum Adami eo sensu posteris imputari affirmavi, quo sensu iis imputari omnes Protestantes constanter tenent. Itaque ille consensum fingeret cum Evangelicis plane falsum: Quis enim unquam Evangelicorum docuit justitiam inhaerentem, quam habemus a Christo, nobis ad justificationem imputari? Quem autem ego profiteor consensum, is verus est, neque negatur, aut negari potest a quoquam non Pelagiano.
latin.170: Tertio denique; Ille prae se ferret tertiam illam justitiae Christi acceptionem pro justitia nobis inhaerente, esse eam, quae intelligitur, cum quaeritur, utrum justitia Christi nobis imputetur, necne? Id quod falsum est. Opponitur enim justitia Christi in ea quaestione nostrae justitiae nobis insitae. Ego vero contra istas acceptiones peccati Adamici, quibus illud imputari dixi consensum esse, removi a statu quaestionis inter nos agitandae, et quidem disertissimis verbis. Quare ab omni ludificatione alienissimus fui.

pass_a.166: GAR. I observe next, that by no necessity, or great utility, the Learned Man was compelled so anxiously and scrupulously to distinguish the subject into four significations; since whoever hitherto have spoken of the imputation of the first sin, have understood nothing else by that name, as can sufficiently appear from their writings, than that actual transgression of the first man himself, by which he violated God's command concerning not tasting the fruit of the forbidden tree. Why then was it needful through laborious windings to lead the reader's mind around, and to make words about sin inhering in us, or our original corruption, and about imputation and the penalty following the guilt itself, concerning which it is sufficiently known that they are by no means treated in this disputation? For it is not asked whether corruption is implanted in us all, on account of which God may deservedly exact penalties from us, or impute it to us, which no one of the Evangelicals ever called back into doubt: That one thing it is delightful to certain ones to call today into Question, whether from that first actual sin of Adam some guilt, and some worthiness of penalty, lies upon the posterity.
pass_a.167: PLAC. First let it be; by no necessity, or great utility, I was compelled so to distinguish Adam's sin, provided the distinction is not false, nor harmful, nor wholly useless, it is enough for me. Would that in his book nothing less true, less useful occurred! Next it is not true, what he says, that whoever have spoken of the imputation of Adam's sin understood nothing else by that name than his actual transgression: of which thing those words of mine ought to have admonished him, and as I use Calvin's words, because it is within us, which, because they obstructed his cause, he deliberately omitted. But those words of Calvin are held Comm. on Rom. 5 vs. 17; you have the whole place above p. 92. For the difference which he observes there between Christ and Adam perishes, unless Adam's sin, which is imputed to us, is within us, and holds itself as a quality inhering in us. Third, What he adds that about inhering sin and its imputation it is not treated in this disputation, that itself I say in this place, and that I might say it I employed that distinction. For that which is not controversial among us had to be separated from that which is controversial, and every ambiguity and confusion had to be removed from this question. Which neglected, those who oppose me in this cause do not assault me, but their own shadow. Finally what he says is called into question, whether from that first actual sin of Adam some guilt and some worthiness of penalty lies upon the posterity, is either false, or does not look to me: For I constantly teach that from that sin some guilt and some worthiness of penalty, if yet it is to be called worthiness, lies upon the posterity: I only wish it to lie not immediately but by the mediating corruption which it produced.
pass_a.168: GAR. But let them say, who display such diligence in explaining the Question, whether they will not reckon it to ludification, and will have it in the place of prestiges, if someone from those New Doctors of the Pontificians, who wish to be believed to go about provinces and cities by zeal of pacification, approaches blandly, and in a momentous cause, say the business of justification, professes consensus with the Evangelicals: that he for his part with not unwilling mind embraces the doctrine of justification through the imputed justice of Christ our Lord, provided it be allowed to explain the matter with a distinction applied; Because namely the justice of Christ can be taken in various modes. 1. For those actions most exact to the rule of the divine law, by which Christ both living and dying rendered fullest obedience to his Father's commands. 2. For that habitual and inhering justice, by which Christ's soul shone most splendidly. 3. For the internal and habitual justice which is subjectively in each of the faithful, but which may deservedly be called Christ's justice, since from Christ, and Christ's Spirit, as author, it flows down into us. In this last sense therefore, he acknowledges, in the controversy of justification, the imputation of Christ's justice: but truly if we take Christ's justice in the first and second signification, he acknowledges no imputation of Christ's justice, but rejects it as absurd. Consensus certainly in this business so explained, there is no one who does not complain that it is a mockery, rather than consensus. &c.
pass_a.169: PLAC. This like thing is not juxtaposed, but opposite. For to this bland prestidigitator I am as dissimilar as white to black. First he would pretend to have enumerated all acceptations of Christ's justice, when yet he would omit one in the business of justification most momentous, by which Christ's justice is taken for that singular obedience which he rendered by suffering death, death, I say, of the cross; which is commonly called passive justice, and is believed without doubt by all Protestants to be imputed to the faithful, when concerning the imputation of active justice, which alone D. Gar. commemorated, there is some discrepancy of opinions, which does not disturb the Church's peace. But I reviewed all acceptations of Adam's first sin, I omitted none. Second he would say that Christ's justice taken in that sense is imputed, in which sense taken it is constantly denied to be imputed by all Protestants. But I affirmed that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity in that sense in which all Protestants constantly hold it is imputed to them. Therefore he would feign a consensus with the Evangelicals plainly false: For who ever of the Evangelicals taught that the inhering justice which we have from Christ is imputed to us unto justification? But the consensus which I profess is true, and is not denied, nor can be denied by anyone not Pelagian.
pass_a.170: Third finally; He would pretend that that third acceptation of Christ's justice for justice inhering in us is that which is understood when it is asked whether Christ's justice is imputed to us, or not? Which is false. For in that question Christ's justice is opposed to our justice implanted in us. But I, against those acceptations of Adamic sin concerning which I said there is consensus that it is imputed, removed them from the status of the question to be agitated among us, and indeed in most clear words. Wherefore I was most alien from every ludification.

166: Garissoles. Next I notice that no necessity, and no great usefulness, drove the learned man to divide the subject so anxiously and scrupulously into four senses. Everyone who has spoken until now of the imputation of the first sin has meant by that name, as their writings sufficiently show, only that actual transgression of the first man by which he broke God's command not to taste the fruit of the forbidden tree. Why then lead the reader through laborious windings, and speak of sin inhering in us—or our original corruption—and of imputation and the penalty that follows guilt, matters everyone knows are not at issue in this dispute? The question is not whether corruption is planted in us all, for which God may justly exact penalties from us or impute it to us—no Evangelical ever called that back into doubt. What some today delight to bring into question is only this: whether from Adam's first actual sin some guilt and some liability to penalty rests on the posterity.
167: Placeus. First grant it: suppose no necessity or great usefulness compelled me to distinguish Adam's sin this way; so long as the distinction is not false, not harmful, and not wholly useless, that is enough for me. Would that nothing less true or less useful appeared in his book! Next, it is not true that everyone who has spoken of imputing Adam's sin meant by that name only his actual transgression. My own words ought to have warned him of that—and Calvin's phrase, "because it is within us," which he deliberately left out because it hindered his case. Those words of Calvin stand in the Commentary on [[Romans 5.17 >> Bible:Romans 5:17]]; you have the whole place above at p. 92. The difference he marks there between Christ and Adam collapses unless Adam's sin, which is imputed to us, is within us and stands as a quality inhering in us. Third, when he adds that inhering sin and its imputation are not treated in this dispute, I say the same here—and I used the distinction so that I could say it. What is not in controversy among us had to be separated from what is, and every ambiguity and confusion cleared from this question. Neglect that, and those who oppose me in this cause do not fight me but their own shadow. Finally, when he says the question raised is whether from Adam's first actual sin some guilt and some liability to penalty rests on the posterity, that is either false or does not touch me: I constantly teach that from that sin some guilt and some liability to penalty—if liability is even the right word—does rest on the posterity. I only insist that it rests not immediately, but through the corruption that sin produced.
168: Garissoles. But let those who parade such care in explaining the Question say whether they will not count it a mockery and a piece of prestidigitation if one of those new Pontifical doctors—who wish to be thought to tour provinces and cities in the zeal of pacification—comes on blandly and, in a weighty cause (say the business of justification), professes agreement with the Evangelicals: that he willingly embraces justification by the imputed righteousness of Christ our Lord, provided he may explain the matter by a distinction. For Christ's righteousness, he would say, can be taken in several ways. (1) For those acts most exact to the rule of God's law, by which Christ living and dying rendered fullest obedience to his Father's commands. (2) For that habitual, inhering righteousness by which Christ's soul shone most splendidly. (3) For the inward, habitual righteousness that is subjectively in each of the faithful, yet may rightly be called Christ's, because it flows into us from Christ and Christ's Spirit as its author. In this last sense, then, he would acknowledge, in the justification controversy, the imputation of Christ's righteousness; but if we take Christ's righteousness in the first and second senses, he would acknowledge no such imputation and reject it as absurd. A consensus in this business so explained—no one fails to complain—is a mockery rather than a consensus. And so on.
169: Placeus. This likeness is not a parallel but an opposite. To that bland prestidigitator I am as unlike as white to black. First, he would pretend to have listed every sense of Christ's righteousness, yet omit the one most decisive in justification: that singular obedience he rendered by suffering death—death, I say, of the cross—which is commonly called passive righteousness and which all Protestants without hesitation believe is imputed to believers, while about imputing active righteousness (the only sense D. Garissoles mentioned) there is some difference of opinion that does not disturb the Church's peace. I, by contrast, reviewed every sense of Adam's first sin and omitted none. Second, he would say that Christ's righteousness, taken in a sense in which all Protestants constantly deny it is imputed, is imputed; whereas I affirmed that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity in the sense in which all Protestants constantly hold it is. So he would invent a plainly false consensus with the Evangelicals: for who among them ever taught that the inhering righteousness we have from Christ is imputed to us for justification? The consensus I profess is true, and no one who is not a Pelagian denies it or can deny it.
170: Third and last: he would pretend that that third sense of Christ's righteousness—as righteousness inhering in us—is what is meant when we ask whether Christ's righteousness is imputed to us or not. That is false. In that question Christ's righteousness is set over against our righteousness implanted in us. I, on the contrary, removed from the state of the question we are debating among ourselves those senses of Adamic sin concerning which I said there is consensus that it is imputed—and I did so in the clearest words. So I stand wholly alien to every mockery.

166.choice: Fourfold distinction needless; first sin = actualis transgressio alone

167.choice: Distinction useful; Calvin intra nos; reatus via mediating corruption

168.choice: Fourfold like Jesuit threefold justitia Christi = ludibrium consensus

169.choice: Analogy opposite; omitted passiva; Placeus consensus true not feigned

170.choice: Third acceptio not the justification question; removed from status; stop before §XIV
